purpose: Documents full-text editorial review of newly downloaded posts before canonical ingestion.

posts.title: Did Jesus Believe in Equality?  You Might Think So….
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that Jesus urges generosity toward people in need without explicitly advocating economic equality or the abolition of private property.
posts.searchSummary: Distinguishes Jesus' concern for people in need from a program of social, political, or economic equality. Examines Luke's Good Samaritan, rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus, and rich ruler narratives, alongside communal ownership in Acts, to show that generosity does not necessarily imply equal possessions. Considers whether differentiated heavenly rewards suggest continuing inequality, while concluding that the Gospels establish neither Jesus' support for complete equality nor his opposition to it.

posts.title: A Very Different (not to say Bizarre) Gospel Featuring Mary Magdalene
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Examines Epiphanius's disputed account of the Greater Questions of Mary and the sexual rituals he attributes to the Gnostic Phibionites.
posts.searchSummary: Introduces the lost Greater Questions of Mary, known only through a hostile account by the heresy hunter Epiphanius. Explains how its alleged portrayal of Jesus teaching Mary through a sexual act relates to Phibionite beliefs about divine sparks trapped in bodies and the avoidance of procreation. Emphasizes that both the document's existence and the rituals attributed to its users remain uncertain because the sole witness was prone to polemical exaggeration and fabrication.

posts.title: Where Christianity Started, And Why – Platinum Guest Post by Peter van Kan
posts.author: Peter van Kan
posts.description: Proposes that Jesus' mystical and healing experiences fostered his messianic self-understanding, shaping the disciples' interpretation of his appearances after death.
posts.searchSummary: Presents Peter van Kan's thesis that Christianity originated in Jesus' developing conviction that he was the Messiah. Attributes that conviction to mystical and healing experiences, the social setting of Galilee, and followers' expectations, rather than to the fulfillment of a divine plan. Argues that the disciples subsequently interpreted experiences of the deceased Jesus through this messianic framework, and that understanding the Gospels requires attention to Jesus' inner life and the author's proposed reality of healing powers.

posts.title: Was Mary Magdalene the Actual Founder of Christianity?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explores whether Mary Magdalene's first proclamation of Jesus' resurrection initiated Christianity, before male leadership overshadowed her role in the movement.
posts.searchSummary: Considers whether Mary Magdalene, rather than Peter, effectively founded Christianity by first proclaiming that Jesus had risen. Argues that traditions crediting an otherwise marginalized woman may preserve historical memory, since later storytellers had stronger incentives to celebrate Peter's authority. Reconstructs Mary's probable Jewish apocalyptic expectations and hope for liberation from oppression, while acknowledging that she left no writings and that her precise beliefs and differences from Peter and Paul cannot be recovered securely.

posts.title: Peter and Mary Magdalene Going Toe to Toe
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Compares competing traditions that give Mary Magdalene or Peter priority as resurrection witnesses and leaders authorized to proclaim the Christian message.
posts.searchSummary: Traces rivalry between Mary Magdalene and Peter through accounts of who first witnessed Jesus' resurrection and received authority to proclaim it. Compares the canonical Gospels with Paul's appearance list in 1 Corinthians, considering whether his omission of women reflects limited knowledge or concerns about testimony. Connects these competing traditions with noncanonical portrayals of Peter challenging Mary's privileged revelations, showing how resurrection testimony intersects with disputes over authority and women's standing.

posts.title: The Intriguing Gospel of Mary Magdalene
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Introduces the Gospel of Mary's account of spiritual liberation and the male disciples' dispute over Mary's authority to convey Jesus' revelation.
posts.searchSummary: Explains the second-century Gospel of Mary, its late discovery and publication, and its portrayal of Mary as the recipient of privileged revelation rather than its claimed author. Describes teachings about matter, the soul's ascent, and escape from bodily passions within the text's Gnostic framework. Follows the concluding dispute in which Andrew and Peter reject Mary's account and Levi defends her authority, highlighting tensions over women's spiritual leadership.

posts.title: Does Paul Ever Refer to (or Even Know About) Judas Iscariot?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that Paul's Last Supper account does not mention Judas's betrayal and leaves uncertain whether Paul knew the betrayal tradition.
posts.searchSummary: Reexamines the translation of paradidomi in 1 Corinthians 11, arguing that Paul probably means God handed Jesus over rather than Judas betrayed him. Considers whether the resurrection appearance to the Twelve implies ignorance of Judas's departure or simply uses a conventional group title. Weighs Paul's contact with Peter against his silence about Judas, concluding that the letters neither establish his knowledge of the betrayal nor securely prove his ignorance.

posts.title: Did Judas Iscariot Actually Exist?  Or Was He “Made Up”?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that independent traditions and the criterion of dissimilarity support Judas's existence and betrayal despite unreliable details in later accounts.
posts.searchSummary: Evaluates the historical evidence for Judas by asking how early, independent, and interested the surviving sources are. Argues that multiple Gospel traditions, Acts, and Papias preserve a widespread account of a disciple betraying Jesus, a story unlikely to have served Christian storytellers' preferred image of their leader. Distinguishes this probable historical core from anti-Jewish stereotypes and the Gospel of Judas's theological agenda, concluding that limited evidence still supports several basic facts.

posts.title: About the Betrayer Judas Iscariot.  What’s an Iscariot?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Surveys proposed meanings of Judas's designation Iscariot and explains why linguistic and geographical uncertainties prevent a secure conclusion about his origins.
posts.searchSummary: Examines whether the designation Iscariot can reveal anything reliable about Judas's background. Reviews derivations involving death, betrayal, complexion, armed resistance, and especially the common proposal that the name means a man from Kerioth. Explains the linguistic objections and uncertainty about the location and continued existence of Kerioth, concluding that neither modern scholars nor possibly the Gospel writers themselves knew the name's meaning with confidence.

posts.title: Slaughter and Human Sacrifice: Understanding Tales of the Hebrew Bible
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Contrasts Jericho's legendary conquest with archaeological evidence and examines Jephthah's daughter within biblical and Greek traditions of human sacrifice.
posts.searchSummary: Challenges the historicity of Joshua's conquest of Jericho by explaining that archaeological evidence does not support a fortified city at the proposed time. Retells Jephthah's sacrifice of his daughter and contrasts it with Abraham's interrupted sacrifice of Isaac, emphasizing the danger of extravagant vows. Places biblical prohibitions and royal child sacrifices alongside the Greek story of Iphigenia to examine the disturbing religious logic of offering a child to a deity.

posts.title: Can You Explain the Tabernacle, the Ark of the Covenant, and/or the Shema?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains the tabernacle and ark as Israel's portable sanctuary and divine throne, then interprets the Shema as exclusive loyalty to Yahweh.
posts.searchSummary: Describes the tabernacle's portable structure, restricted sacred spaces, and the ark's function as God's earthly throne and repository for the covenant tablets. Explains priestly access to the holy of holies and the significance of the Day of Atonement. Interprets the Shema in Deuteronomy as a demand that Israel worship and love Yahweh alone, rather than necessarily deny other gods' existence, and notes its continuing importance for Jewish faith and Jesus' teaching.

posts.title: Jesus’s Salvation, Self-Identity, and Birth: Key Questions from Readers
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains Paul's language of faith, distinguishes Jesus' divine sonship from claims to be God, and evaluates rumors about Jesus' parentage.
posts.searchSummary: Answers three reader questions about salvation, Jesus' self-identity, and his birth. Favors interpreting Paul's faith-of-Christ language as believers' faith in Jesus, and distinguishes the Synoptics' Son of God claims from John's portrayal of a preexistent divine figure. Considers whether virgin-birth traditions countered rumors of conception outside marriage, while stressing that the historical reconstruction is uncertain and that there is virtually no evidence Mary was a sex worker.

posts.title: Do You Really Mean That?  Antisemitism.
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues for distinguishing religious anti-Judaism from racial antisemitism to clarify different historical forms of hostility and violence against Jewish people.
posts.searchSummary: Advocates a precise distinction between opposition to Jewish religion or culture and hostility based on inherited Jewish ancestry. Traces Christian anti-Judaism through forced conversion and persecution, contrasting it with modern racial theories and Nazi persecution of people regardless of their beliefs. Argues that collapsing these categories, or automatically applying racial terminology to criticism of Israeli policies, obscures different historical mechanisms of violence; this reflects the author's explicitly narrow use of antisemitism.

posts.title: A Blog Dinner in Denver, CO on November 19.  Interested?
posts.author: jennao
posts.description: Invites blog members to a small Denver dinner with Bart Ehrman and Jen Olmos during the Society of Biblical Literature meeting.
posts.searchSummary: Announces a proposed blog-member dinner in Denver on November 19 while Bart Ehrman and Jen Olmos attend the Society of Biblical Literature meeting. Describes an informal gathering for conversation, with attendees responsible for travel and their own meals and no expertise required. Requests advance contact by email rather than comments because space is limited, while leaving the exact time and restaurant near the convention center to be determined.

posts.title: Do You Really Mean That?  Consciousness and Socialism
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Urges greater precision in discussing consciousness and socialism, distinguishing subjective awareness from responsiveness and collective ownership from social-democratic policy.
posts.searchSummary: Reflects on how imprecise language obstructs discussion of consciousness and economic policy. Uses Michael Pollan's treatment of plants to distinguish responsiveness to stimuli from subjective awareness, without claiming to settle whether plants are conscious. Separately argues that contemporary American proposals labeled democratic socialism often resemble social democracy rather than collective ownership, emphasizing clarity of terminology instead of endorsing or rejecting the scientific and political positions under discussion.

posts.title: The Ten (more or less?) Commandments and the Code of Hammurabi
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Compares Jewish and Christian numbering of the Ten Commandments and illustrates similarities and differences between biblical laws and Hammurabi's earlier code.
posts.searchSummary: Shows that the Ten Commandments are divided differently in Jewish, Protestant and Orthodox, and Catholic and Lutheran traditions. Explains that Israelite legal collections were not unique, introducing the much older Code of Hammurabi as a comparative source. Quotes laws concerning sexual conduct, family authority, bodily injury, and compensation to illustrate both familiar principles and striking differences, including penalties shaped by social status rather than a uniform standard for all people.

posts.title: The Origins of God’s Personal Name and of the Feast of Passover
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Examines Exodus's explanations of God's name and traces Passover's development from an agricultural festival into a commemoration of liberation from Egypt.
posts.searchSummary: Explores the relationship between YHWH and the Hebrew verb meaning to be through the three explanations of God's name in Exodus 3. Emphasizes uncertainty about the exact derivation and interpretation rather than treating one explanation as settled. Separately traces Passover's probable agricultural origins, its association with the exodus and unleavened bread, and the symbolic meal and Jerusalem observance that form an important setting for Jesus' final days.

posts.title: Important Questions About Jesus, Paul, and the Gospels
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Defends the evidence for Jesus' imminent apocalyptic expectations, addresses claims about sacrifice and vegetarianism, and assesses Paul's possible influence on the Gospels.
posts.searchSummary: Answers questions about Jesus' expectation of the end, alleged opposition to animal sacrifice, and Paul's influence on Gospel theology. Treats imminent apocalyptic expectation as a conclusion from critically assessed traditions, and finds no convincing evidence that Jesus was a principled vegetarian. Compares Gospel treatments of law, atonement, and belief with Paul's views, emphasizing that theological similarities or differences do not establish direct use of his letters or even awareness of their source.

posts.title: Health, Wealth, and the Prosperity Gospel
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Traces prosperity preaching through Oral Roberts and Russell Conwell, contrasting promised divine returns with wealth earned through work and used for charity.
posts.searchSummary: Explores the transition from faith healing to prosperity preaching through Oral Roberts's promise that faithful giving produces material returns. Contrasts this with Russell Conwell's earlier message that Christians should become wealthy through hard work, while examining his harsh judgments of poverty. Notes that Conwell gave away much of his own earnings for education, complicating the contrast between pursuing riches and using wealth to help others; comparison with Jesus' teachings is reserved for later posts.

posts.title: How to Justify a Lie
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Challenges Salvian's defenses of writing as Timothy and argues that seeking an authoritative hearing explains his deliberate deception about authorship.
posts.searchSummary: Evaluates Salvian's claim that Timothy was merely a symbolic pen name chosen to honor God, despite his admission that an obscure author would lack authority. Challenges modern explanations based on humility, noting that anonymity could have served that purpose and that Salvian also published under his own name. Uses Bishop Salonius's objection and Salvian's inconsistent defenses to argue that ancient forgery sought authority through deception and was not simply an accepted literary convention.

posts.title: Caught Red-Handed!  An Unrepentant Christian Forger
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Recounts Salvian's exposure as the author of a letter attributed to Timothy and examines his contradictory attempts to justify the deception.
posts.searchSummary: Uses the fifth-century presbyter Salvian's forged letter from Timothy to challenge claims that ancient readers accepted false authorial attribution. Recounts how Bishop Salonius confronted Salvian and how the surviving defense both dismisses authors' names as unimportant and invokes borrowed prestige to secure readers' attention. Explains the tension between this appeal to apostolic authority and Salvian's claim that Timothy was only a symbolic pen name, setting up a further critique of his excuses.
